description: ADR-0025. A rule that declares alternative ATT&CK techniques establishes none of the alternatives by default. Each decision below records, for one source rule that was read, exactly the techniques every match of it establishes, and why. A decision can only name techniques the rule declares; an empty list says the rule's logic cannot establish its technique (its detections are still shown, as declared only).

decisions.rule_name: Potential LSASS Process Dump Via Procdump
decisions.reason: Every branch requires the full-memory-dump flag and a target beginning 'ls' on the command line: that is a dump of LSASS memory whatever the binary is called. Nothing in the rule tests that the binary was renamed, so Masquerading is not established by a match.

decisions.rule_name: Potential Credential Access via LSASS Memory Dump
decisions.reason: The rule matches a process-access event whose target is lsass.exe with a memory-dump library in the call trace: an LSASS memory dump. Native API names the mechanism the author had in mind; the match does not separately establish it.
The rule matches a script host started with a .vbs script: Visual Basic execution. What the script then discovers is not observed by the rule, so Group Policy Discovery is not established by a match.

decisions.rule_name: Registry Tampering by Potentially Suspicious Processes
decisions.reason: Every branch matches a registry value being set: Modify Registry. The setting process differs by branch (several script hosts and utilities), so Visual Basic is not established by every match.

decisions.rule_name: Hidden Executable In NTFS Alternate Data Stream
decisions.reason: The rule matches any stream-creation event whose file hash has an import hash, i.e. whenever a stream is created on an executable. It does not test that the stream is a named alternate data stream. Inspected on a lab recording: it fired on a browser saving a downloaded executable (the event names the file, no alternate stream, no stream contents). That event matters - it is the download of the payload - but it does not show an executable hidden in an alternate data stream.

decisions.rule_name: Potential PowerShell HackTool Script by Function Names
decisions.reason: A script block is logged when PowerShell compiles code to run it, so every match is PowerShell execution. Which of the many listed offensive functions is present differs by match, so none of the other declared techniques is established by every match.

decisions.rule_name: Command and Scripting Interpreter via Windows Scripts
decisions.reason: Every match is a command interpreter (PowerShell or cmd) started by a script host (wscript or mshta). Which interpreter, which script language and whether mshta was the parent differ by match, so no single sub-technique is established.
Every match is a powershell.exe process start. The obfuscation, download and decoding patterns are alternatives on the command line, so none of them is established by every match.

Every match is a command shell started directly by the service control manager: a command run through a service. Which shell differs by match; that a service was created or modified is not observed by this rule.
The rule matches a file being written whose name is that of a credential-dumping tool or its output. A file name does not show which credential store, if any, was dumped.

decisions.rule_name: Potential Antimalware Scan Interface Bypass via PowerShell
decisions.reason: A script block is logged when PowerShell compiles code to run it, so every match is PowerShell execution. The rule looks for strings associated with AMSI tampering; several of them also occur in code that only inspects AMSI, so tampering and obfuscation are not established by every match.

decisions.rule_name: Suspicious Service was Installed in the System
decisions.reason: Every branch is a service-installation event (Security 4697 or System 7045) with a suspicious service binary: a Windows service was created. That the service then ran a command is not observed by this rule.

decisions.rule_name: PowerShell Suspicious Script with Clipboard Retrieval Capabilities
decisions.reason: A script block is logged when PowerShell compiles code to run it, so every match is PowerShell execution. Every branch requires a call that reads the clipboard, so Clipboard Data is established as well.

A script block is logged when PowerShell compiles code to run it, so every match is PowerShell execution. Every branch requires keystroke-capture calls (key-state polling, or a keyboard hook with window tracking). Native API names the mechanism and is not separately established.
Every branch is an archiving utility adding files to an archive with a password option: Archive via Utility. Where the archived data came from is not observed.

A script block is logged when PowerShell compiles code to run it, so every match is PowerShell execution. The matched strings define types for calling native functions; that a native function was then called is not observed.
The rule matches the tool's file name alone. Neither what was dumped nor a renamed binary is observed.
The rule matches a rundll32 command line with no arguments. That is a known sign of a sacrificial process but shows none of the three declared techniques by itself.

Read from the logic, every branch is a registry value of Microsoft Defender being set to a disabling value, which looked like both declared techniques at once. The matched event in a lab recording showed otherwise: the process setting the value was Defender's own engine. The rule does not tell an adversary changing these values from the product managing its own settings, so neither technique is established by every match. (First recorded as establishing both; corrected after the event was inspected.)

Every branch is a command line containing a base64-decoding call (plain or in an encoded command): decoding at run time. The rule does not test which program was started, so PowerShell is not established by the rule itself.

decisions.rule_name: PowerShell Suspicious Script with Screenshot Capabilities
decisions.reason: A script block is logged when PowerShell compiles code to run it, so every match is PowerShell execution. The rule requires a screen-copy call together with a bitmap type, so Screen Capture is established as well.

decisions.rule_name: Remote LSASS Process Access Through Windows Remote Management
decisions.reason: Every match is the WinRM provider host process opening LSASS: Windows Remote Management is in use. Opening the process is not a memory dump, and the PowerShell session is implied, not observed.
Every match is the WinRM provider host process, as the image or the parent: a remote-management session. PowerShell is the usual plug-in but the rule does not observe it.

decisions.rule_name: Mounting Hidden or WebDav Remote Shares
decisions.reason: Read in full: net.exe or net1.exe with 'use' and a target that is a hidden share, a WebDAV share over SSL, or an http location, excluding deletions. The three kinds of target are alternatives, and the translated branches keep the hidden-share and WebDAV patterns together, so a match does not say which was mounted. Mounting a WebDAV location is not SMB/Windows Admin Shares, and nothing in the rule observes which account was used or any account discovery. Inspected events (47, one recording): every one mounted an administrative share of another host with supplied credentials - those events are SMB/Windows Admin Shares, but the rule cannot establish that for every match. That technique is established there by another rule; nothing is lost in that recording. A decision conditioned on the matched event would recover it in general and is not supported yet.

Read in full: a child of the service control manager that either echoes a value into a named pipe or runs rundll32 on a DLL with the ',a /p:' arguments - the two published named-pipe impersonation methods of the getsystem command. Both are Token Impersonation/Theft; neither branch observes a new process being created with the token. Inspected events (two recordings): the second branch exactly, a temporary DLL run by rundll32 under services.exe.

left_ambiguous_after_reading.rule_name: Potential Credential Access via Windows Utilities
left_ambiguous_after_reading.why: Several dump utilities; the procdump branch does not test which process is dumped.
Matches the PsExec client by name; PsExec also runs commands locally.

left_ambiguous_after_reading.rule_name: Potential Arbitrary Command Execution Via FTP.EXE
left_ambiguous_after_reading.why: One branch is a child of ftp.exe, the other only an ftp script option.
A memory dump through comsvcs.dll; the rule does not test which process is dumped.
